title: Bioconductor Community Handbook
text:
Welcome
Welcome to the Bioconductor Community Handbook.
Whether you are part of the Bioconductor community, work with a neighbouring project, or are discovering these communities for the first time, this handbook is for you. We hope it helps you find your way around shared practices, resources, and conversations, and supports you in contributing to open, inclusive, and collaborative bioinformatics.

title: Bioconductor Community Handbook
text:
What this book is
This book was initiated during a BioFAIR Collaboration Fest held at The Open University on 15-17 September 2026.
The handbook began as an effort to capture FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) practices not covered by existing Bioconductor materials. Cross-community discussions broadened its scope into a handbook bringing together key aspects of community practice in one place.
The structure of this handbook is inspired from The Turing Way, with sections dedicated to:

Guide to package development
Guide to package maintenance
Guide to package peer review
Guide to communication
Guide to FAIR practices

title: 4  Guide to communication
text:
4.1 Overview
This guide will provide practical advice for communicating within the Bioconductor community and with other communities.
It will define shared language, identify where to ask questions and share needs, and describe how users, developers, trainers, and maintainers can collaborate effectively within and beyond Bioconductor.

title: 5  Communicating across communities
text: This section will introduce communication practices, resources, and pathways for coordinating work within the community and building effective relationships with other projects and communities.

title: 6  Guide to FAIR
text:
6.1 Overview
As part of the Bioconductor community, we develop and maintain open-source software, data, and training resources. By applying the FAIR principles – Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable – this guide will cover practices and resources supporting users and developers in making those resources easier to discover, access, integrate, and reuse within and beyond the Bioconductor ecosystem. The following sections describe processes, resources, and checklists for producing FAIR Bioconductor tools, wrappers and workflows, including integrations with other software ecosystems.

title: 7  Interoperable file types
text: Preferred file types for disk-based storage of R objects and interoperability with other programming languages and software ecosystems will be documented here.

title: 8  Bioconductor in Galaxy
section: 8.3 Galaxy file types for Bioconductor objects
text:
8.3 Galaxy file types for Bioconductor objects
How are R objects stored on disk in Galaxy? What are the preferred file types for interoperability with other programming languages and software ecosystems?
For example, this GitHub issue has been discussing insecure aspects of RData files. While those are the default file type for R objects, they are not interoperable with other programming languages and software ecosystems. Instead, the loom file format has gained popularity as a preferred file type for disk-based storage of R objects, and is interoperable with other programming languages and software ecosystems
